error_modes.label: LEVEL OFF ALTITUDE AT PATTERN ALTITUDE

texts.0: SP, due to the absence of a lead point for the level off in the climbing turn, did not arrest the climb at pattern altitude as required by the specific criteria. The aircraft passed more than 300 feet above the assigned pattern altitude and was still climbing when the IP took the controls to stop the overshoot. The return to pattern altitude was flown by the IP and not by SP.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction after the roll out on downwind, did not complete the level off at pattern altitude within tolerance. Altitude reached the 300 feet limit above the assigned value and stayed there until the IP prompted verbally. SP corrected only after that call, so the level off was finished late and the downwind was flown high for several seconds.
texts.2: SP, due to slow relaxation of back pressure during the roll out, did not stop the climb at the assigned pattern altitude on the first attempt. Altitude deviated about 200 feet high, between the 150 and the 300 feet band. SP identified the trend without any prompting and re-established pattern altitude within a few seconds with no IP input.
texts.3: SP set the lead point in good time, reduced power and relaxed back pressure so that the level off was completed within 150 feet of the assigned pattern altitude. Altitude was then held steady while SP re-established downwind spacing. Pitch and power were adjusted in one continuous sequence rather than by successive corrections.
texts.4: SP anticipated the level off and stopped the climb within about 50 feet of pattern altitude, with no overshoot and no secondary correction. Altitude then remained essentially constant for the whole downwind leg. The transition from climb to level flight was made with a single smooth control and power input.
texts.marginal: SP levelled off inside the required tolerance, but each pattern finished about 130 feet above the assigned altitude and needed a small secondary correction to settle. The deviation was in the same direction every time, which shows the lead point is being set late rather than misjudged at random. SP is expected to anticipate the level off earlier so that pattern altitude is captured on the first input.

error_modes.label: BANK AND AIRSPEED CONTROL DURING THE MANEUVER

texts.0: SP, due to uncoordinated application of bank and back pressure at the initiation of the closed pattern, did not maintain the bank and the airspeeds prescribed by the Flight Manual and the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Bank increased about 25 deg past the briefed value while airspeed decayed well below the value for the turn, and the aircraft arrived on downwind low on energy and displaced from the intended track. The IP reduced bank and reset the flight path before the pattern could be continued.
texts.1: SP, due to chasing the flight path with bank instead of stabilizing pitch first, did not hold the bank and airspeeds of the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Bank varied about 15 deg either side of the briefed value and airspeed sat at the low limit for the turn until the IP called for a correction. SP recovered the parameters only after that verbal input, so the pattern was flown at the edge of the standard throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to a lagging cross-check between attitude and airspeed in the turn, did not hold the briefed bank and airspeed continuously. Bank wandered about 10 deg around the briefed value with a corresponding airspeed excursion, which left the aircraft between the 150 and 300 feet band on the subsequent level off. SP detected both deviations early and re-established the parameters without prompting and without IP action.
texts.3: SP established the briefed bank at the initiation and held it accurately, with airspeed maintained within the values of the Flight Manual and the Techniques and Procedures Manual throughout the turn. The cross-check between attitude, bank and airspeed remained continuous, so corrections were small and made early. The aircraft arrived on downwind on the intended track and on speed.
texts.4: SP flew the closed pattern with the bank set precisely at the briefed value and held it essentially constant, with airspeed steady inside the prescribed range from initiation to roll out. No corrective input beyond trim adjustment was needed at any point of the turn. The aircraft arrived on downwind on speed, on altitude and on the intended track.
texts.marginal: SP kept bank and airspeed inside the standards, but the bank was consistently a few degrees shallow and airspeed drifted toward the low end of the range in the second half of the turn. The pattern remained acceptable only because SP added power late each time. SP is expected to set the briefed bank at the initiation and protect the airspeed with the power setting rather than by unloading the turn.

error_modes.label: DOWNWIND ENTRY, TRAFFIC SEQUENCING AND MINIMUM ENTRY AIRSPEED

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft position in the pattern, did not enter downwind according to the existing traffic and did not respect the 140 KIAS minimum entry airspeed. The aircraft rolled out on downwind at 126 KIAS and inside the preceding aircraft, with no usable spacing for the following approach. The IP took control to restore separation and to re-establish the aircraft on the correct downwind position.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness of the traffic already established in the pattern, did not adjust the closed pattern to the existing traffic and entered downwind at 140 KIAS with no margin. Spacing on the preceding aircraft was reduced to the point where the IP had to call for an extension of the downwind. SP acted only after that call, so the sequence was preserved by verbal direction rather than by SP planning.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that stayed inside the cockpit during the turn, did not confirm the position of the preceding traffic before initiating the closed pattern. Airspeed on entering downwind was 145 KIAS, above the minimum but with the spacing tighter than briefed. SP identified the closure on the preceding aircraft in good time and adjusted the downwind track and power without prompting and without IP input.
texts.3: SP checked the pattern traffic before initiating and entered downwind clear of the preceding aircraft with an airspeed comfortably above the 140 KIAS minimum. Spacing supported a normal continuation to the following approach with no adjustment required. The lookout was maintained throughout the turn as well as on the downwind.
texts.4: SP built the closed pattern around the traffic already established, timing the initiation so that the downwind entry produced correct spacing with no later adjustment. Airspeed on entering downwind was well above the 140 KIAS minimum and stable. SP kept an accurate picture of every aircraft in the pattern and reported it correctly when asked.
texts.marginal: SP entered downwind above the 140 KIAS minimum and clear of traffic, but the decision to initiate was taken late each time and the spacing came out tighter than briefed. The picture of the preceding aircraft was rebuilt during the turn rather than established before it. SP is expected to confirm the traffic sequence before initiating the closed pattern so that the downwind entry needs no further adjustment.

error_modes.label: POWER MANAGEMENT AND ENERGY THROUGH THE PATTERN

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete power lever movement at the initiation, did not set MAX power as required and did not adjust power afterwards as the pattern demanded. The aircraft entered the turn with a partial power setting and lost the energy required for the climbing turn, arriving below pattern altitude and slow. The IP advanced the power lever and reset the profile before the pattern could be completed.
texts.1: SP, due to setting power by feel instead of confirming the indication, did not set MAX power at the initiation of the closed pattern. Torque remained short of the required value for most of the climbing turn and airspeed decayed to the lower limit until the IP called for power. SP made the correction only after that call, and the level off was consequently reached at the 300 feet tolerance.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction after the level off, did not adjust power as required once pattern altitude was reached. The aircraft accelerated through the briefed downwind speed and finished about 200 feet high before the correction took effect. SP recognized the excess energy without prompting and set the correct power to restore both altitude and speed with no IP input.
texts.3: SP set MAX power at the initiation, confirmed the indication and then adjusted power as required at the level off so that the downwind was flown at the briefed setting. Energy through the pattern was managed with anticipation rather than with reactive corrections. Altitude and airspeed were both re-established within tolerance at the same time.
texts.4: SP applied MAX power smoothly and precisely at the initiation and reduced it at exactly the point required for the level off, so that pattern altitude and downwind airspeed were captured together with no overshoot. Power changes were small, timely and matched to the flight path throughout the pattern. No further adjustment was needed during the downwind.
texts.marginal: SP set MAX power at the initiation and adjusted afterwards inside the standards, but the reduction at the level off was made in two steps and slightly late on each pattern. This left a small altitude and speed excursion that had to be corrected on the downwind. SP is expected to plan the power reduction with the level off so that both parameters are captured with a single adjustment.

error_modes.label: STALL MARGIN AND AVOIDANCE OF STALL CHARACTERISTICS

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn, increased back pressure to hold the flight path and allowed the onset of stall characteristics. Airframe buffet developed with the stall warning active while the aircraft was banked and climbing, and the margin above the stall was lost rather than protected. The IP took control, unloaded the aircraft and recovered the energy state.
texts.1: SP, due to workload management that left the radio call and the power setting to be completed inside the turn, allowed airspeed to decay to the point where the initial stall warning was heard. SP did not unload the aircraft until the IP called for it, so the margin was restored by direction and not by SP recognition. The pattern was continued only after the energy state had been re-established.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the traffic during the turn, allowed airspeed to fall toward the low end of the range for the bank being flown. The margin above the stall was reduced although no stall warning or buffet occurred. SP recognized the decay early, reduced bank and added power without prompting, and the aircraft was returned to the briefed airspeed with no IP input.
texts.3: SP protected the stall margin throughout the closed pattern by matching bank and back pressure to the available power, and no stall characteristics of any kind appeared. Airspeed stayed inside the prescribed range for the bank being flown at every stage of the turn. Secondary tasks were kept out of the highest workload part of the maneuver.
texts.4: SP flew the closed pattern with an ample and constant margin above the stall, with airspeed stable in the upper part of the prescribed range and no buffet or warning indication at any point. Workload was sequenced so that the turn required only flying, with radio and cockpit tasks completed before and after it. The energy state was managed with clear anticipation throughout.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft clear of stall characteristics, but the airspeed reached the lower end of the acceptable range in the second half of each turn before power was added. The margin remained legal while depending on a late correction rather than on planning. SP is expected to sequence the cockpit tasks outside the turn and to protect the airspeed with power from the initiation.

texts.0: SP, due to reliance on how the maneuver is habitually flown rather than on the published criteria, did not follow the standard procedure of the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the LAP. The closed pattern was initiated without the required clearance and the ground track was flown outside the published pattern limits, with the checks and calls of the procedure omitted. The IP intervened, took control and returned the aircraft to the published pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to an unwritten local practice followed in place of the published procedure, did not execute the closed pattern in the sequence prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the LAP. Two required actions were taken out of order and the associated call was made late, which left the pattern at the limit of the published profile until the IP directed the correct sequence. SP complied only after that verbal direction.
texts.2: SP, due to reverting to the habitual sequence rather than the one published for the pattern in use, did not perform the required actions in the correct order at the initiation of the closed pattern. One item of the sequence was completed late in relation to the published procedure, with the resulting altitude deviation inside the 150 to 300 feet band. SP identified the omission on its own and completed the sequence correctly with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the closed pattern in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the applicable LAP, initiating only under the specified conditions and with the required clearance. The sequence of checks, configuration and calls was completed in the correct order and at the correct points. The published ground track was respected throughout.
texts.4: SP executed the closed pattern exactly to the published procedure, with every check, configuration change and call made at the correct point without hesitation and without any reminder. The pattern was flown precisely on the LAP ground track under the specified conditions. SP also stated the applicable procedure correctly when questioned in the debrief.
texts.marginal: SP followed the published procedure and the LAP, but the calls and the required actions were made at the very end of their correct window on each pattern. The sequence was correct in content and consistently late in timing, which compressed the remaining part of the maneuver. SP is expected to complete each item at its published point so that the pattern is not flown under self-imposed time pressure.

error_modes.label: DOWNWIND DISPLACEMENT COMPARED WITH THE OVERHEAD BREAK PATTERN

texts.0: SP, due to a climbing turn flown without reference to the downwind displacement established with an overhead break, did not roll out on the standard downwind track. The aircraft ended up well outside the published downwind line and more than 300 feet off pattern altitude while the runway sight picture was still being searched for. The IP took the controls and repositioned the aircraft on the standard downwind before the pattern could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to holding the initial 60 degrees of bank without checking the runway sight picture, did not match the downwind displacement of the overhead break pattern. Roll out occurred wide of the standard downwind track and altitude reached the 300 feet limit above pattern altitude while the leg was being re-intercepted. The correction was started only after the IP called the displacement.
texts.2: SP, due to a late comparison between the runway sight picture and the displacement used in the overhead break, rolled out slightly outside the standard downwind track. The correction back to the published line left altitude about 200 feet off pattern altitude, between the 150 and 300 feet band. SP recognized the wide roll out early and re-established the correct displacement without prompting and without IP action.
texts.3: SP flew the climbing turn to arrive on the same downwind displacement as the overhead break pattern, using the runway sight picture to judge the roll out point. Track and spacing matched the standard downwind and altitude stayed within 150 feet of pattern altitude throughout. Only small heading adjustments were needed after the roll out.
texts.4: SP rolled out on the standard downwind line, with the displacement indistinguishable from a pattern entered by the overhead break. Altitude at roll out was within about 50 feet of pattern altitude and no lateral correction was required. Spacing for the following approach was set at the roll out and needed no adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP rolled out inside the pattern limits, but the downwind was consistently a little wider than the displacement established with the overhead break and each pattern needed a shallow correction back to the line. Altitude remained inside tolerance only because that correction was flown level. SP is expected to use the runway sight picture during the climbing turn so that the roll out falls on the standard downwind displacement at the first attempt.

error_modes.label: VERTICAL SPEED AT LEVEL OFF AND USE OF BANK UP TO 90 DEGREES

texts.0: SP, due to MAX power carried into a climb rate far higher than the level off could absorb, did not use the available bank to arrest the vertical speed as the manual provides. The climb was still established at pattern altitude and the aircraft passed more than 300 feet above it before any pitch or power change was made. The IP took the controls, reduced power and rolled into bank to stop the climb.
texts.1: SP, due to attempting to stop an excessive vertical speed with pitch alone, did not increase bank toward 90 degrees to affect the level off. The climb was arrested only at the 300 feet limit above pattern altitude and after the IP called for more bank. The aircraft was then held level, but the level off was completed late and high.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction that left the vertical speed high approaching pattern altitude, did not initially use bank to help arrest the climb. Altitude overshot about 200 feet, between the 150 and 300 feet band, before the climb was stopped. SP increased bank without prompting, re-established pattern altitude promptly and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP recognized the high vertical speed during the climbing turn and increased bank toward the 90 degree maximum to affect the level off, together with the power reduction. The climb was arrested within 150 feet of pattern altitude and the aircraft stayed inside the pattern limits. Bank was reduced again as soon as the vertical speed came under control.
texts.4: SP controlled the vertical speed from the start of the climbing turn, so the level off required only a small increase of bank well inside the 90 degree maximum. Pattern altitude was captured within about 50 feet with no overshoot. The return to normal bank and the power reduction were made as a single coordinated sequence.
texts.marginal: SP arrested the climb inside tolerance, but the vertical speed was allowed to build every time and only an increase of bank close to the 90 degree maximum kept the level off within limits. The technique worked, yet it consumed the whole margin of the published correction. SP is expected to control the climb rate with power earlier so that bank is a refinement of the level off and not the only means of stopping the climb.

error_modes.label: PULL-UP ATTITUDE AND RUDDER IN THE DIRECTION OF THE TURN

texts.0: SP, due to a pull-up taken well beyond the fire light on the horizon reference, did not begin the climbing turn from a controllable nose attitude. The nose stayed high with the bank slow to develop, airspeed decayed toward the 140 KIAS minimum and the aircraft climbed more than 300 feet through pattern altitude in an unstable attitude. The IP took the controls, lowered the nose and re-established the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to an excessively nose-high pull-up, did not apply a small amount of rudder in the direction of the turn to bring the nose back to the horizon. The nose came down only after the IP called for the correction and the level off finished at the 300 feet limit above pattern altitude. Airspeed sat at the low end of the range for most of the climbing turn.
texts.2: SP, due to back pressure applied past the fire light on the horizon picture, allowed the nose to rise above the intended pull-up attitude at the initiation. A small amount of rudder in the direction of the turn was used to bring the nose back to the horizon, but the trajectory left the aircraft about 200 feet high, between the 150 and 300 feet band. The correction was made without prompting and the pattern continued normally.
texts.3: SP pulled the nose up to approximately the fire light on the horizon and began the climbing turn from that attitude, so no exaggerated nose-high condition developed. Airspeed stayed above the 140 KIAS minimum and the level off was completed within 150 feet of pattern altitude. Rudder was used only to keep the turn coordinated.
texts.4: SP set the pull-up attitude at the fire light on the horizon reference and rolled into the climbing turn in one continuous movement. The nose never went beyond the reference, so no rudder correction toward the horizon was needed and altitude was captured within about 50 feet. Airspeed remained comfortably inside the range throughout.
texts.marginal: SP kept the pattern inside limits, but the pull-up went slightly above the fire light on the horizon at each attempt and needed rudder in the direction of the turn to recover the picture. Airspeed dropped toward the lower part of the range every time before it recovered. SP is expected to stop the pull-up at the reference attitude rather than to correct a nose-high condition after it has developed.

error_modes.label: POWER REDUCTION TO 20 PERCENT TORQUE AND DOWNWIND SPEED 140 TO 150 KIAS

texts.0: SP, due to MAX power left set through the level off instead of the PCL being retarded to approximately 20 percent torque, did not prevent the acceleration approaching pattern altitude. The aircraft ended more than 300 feet above pattern altitude and then accelerated far beyond the 140 to 150 KIAS downwind band with no power correction made. The IP reduced power and re-established both altitude and airspeed on downwind.
texts.1: SP, due to a power reduction made after the roll out instead of approaching pattern altitude, did not stabilize the downwind inside the 140 to 150 KIAS band. Airspeed ran about 20 knots above the band and altitude reached the 300 feet limit before the PCL was brought back toward 20 percent torque. The reduction was made only after the IP called the excess speed.
texts.2: SP, due to a partial power reduction that left torque well above the approximately 20 percent target, did not arrest the acceleration at the level off in one movement. Airspeed overshot the 140 to 150 KIAS band by about 10 knots and altitude sat around 200 feet high, between the 150 and 300 feet band. SP cross-checked the torque indication, completed the reduction and stabilized the downwind with no IP input.
texts.3: SP reduced power approaching pattern altitude to prevent the acceleration and retarded the PCL to approximately 20 percent torque at the level off. Altitude was held within 150 feet of pattern altitude and airspeed settled inside the 140 to 150 KIAS band on downwind. The torque indication was cross-checked after the reduction rather than assumed.
texts.4: SP anticipated the level off, reduced power so that no acceleration developed and set approximately 20 percent torque in a single movement. The downwind stabilized within a few knots of the planned value inside the 140 to 150 KIAS band, with altitude within about 50 feet. No further power adjustment was needed for the rest of the leg.
texts.marginal: SP kept altitude and airspeed inside the standards, but the power reduction was always slightly late and torque was left above the approximately 20 percent value, so the downwind stabilized only at the top of the 140 to 150 KIAS band. Each pattern needed a second small reduction before the speed settled. SP is expected to begin the reduction approaching pattern altitude and to cross-check the torque setting so that the leg stabilizes on the first input.

error_modes.label: CLOSED TO LOW KEY: LEVEL OFF AT 1500 FEET AGL, SPACING AND HIGH DOWNWIND REPORT
error_modes.source: technique:5.38 ADDITIONAL OPTIONS FOR ELP TRAINING

texts.0: SP, due to a closed to Low Key flown with the picture of a normal closed pattern and no reference to 1,500 feet AGL, did not reduce power on reaching that altitude. The aircraft passed more than 300 feet through the intended level off with spacing unconfirmed and the high downwind report omitted. The IP took the controls, reduced power and re-established the profile toward Low Key.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction on reaching 1,500 feet AGL, did not level the closed to Low Key at the intended altitude and did not confirm proper spacing before reporting. Altitude reached the 300 feet limit above 1,500 feet AGL and the high downwind report was made only after the IP prompted. The profile was then regained, but the run to Low Key started high.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the spacing check while the aircraft was still climbing, did not stop the climb at 1,500 feet AGL at the first attempt. Altitude deviated about 200 feet high, between the 150 and 300 feet band, before power was reduced. SP recognized the deviation, returned to 1,500 feet AGL and made the high downwind report per local guidance without prompting.
texts.3: SP levelled the closed to Low Key at 1,500 feet AGL, reduced power as required and confirmed proper spacing before reporting high downwind per local guidance. Altitude was held within 150 feet of the target and the profile stayed set up for a normal arrival at Low Key. The spacing check was made without any loss of aircraft control.
texts.4: SP arrived at 1,500 feet AGL with the climb already under control and captured the altitude within about 50 feet, with power reduced in one movement. Spacing was confirmed and the high downwind report was made at the correct point per local guidance. The profile continued to Low Key with no further altitude or spacing correction.
texts.marginal: SP levelled inside tolerance, but the closed to Low Key finished consistently high on 1,500 feet AGL and the spacing check was made after, not before, the high downwind report. The profile stayed workable only because the following descent absorbed the excess altitude. SP is expected to lead the level off at 1,500 feet AGL and to confirm spacing before making the report.

error_modes.label: CLOSED TO LOW KEY: CONFIGURATION BELOW 147 KIAS AND 120 KIAS TO LOW KEY
error_modes.source: technique:5.38 ADDITIONAL OPTIONS FOR ELP TRAINING

texts.0: SP, due to the deceleration below 147 KIAS never being monitored after the level off, did not lower the gear and takeoff flaps at the point required for the closed to Low Key. The aircraft arrived unconfigured and more than 300 feet off the intended profile, with airspeed uncontrolled instead of held at 120 KIAS minimum. The IP took the controls, configured the aircraft and re-established the ELP profile.
texts.1: SP, due to attention on the ground track instead of the airspeed, did not lower the gear and takeoff flaps once the aircraft had decelerated below 147 KIAS. The configuration was completed only after the IP called for it and the aircraft reached Low Key at the 300 feet limit above the intended profile with the speed still well above 120 KIAS. The rest of the pattern was flown catching up with the profile.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow cross-check of the airspeed against the 147 KIAS gate, delayed the gear and takeoff flap selection by several seconds after the aircraft had decelerated. The additional drag arrived late and left the aircraft about 200 feet high, between the 150 and 300 feet band, on the way to Low Key. SP identified the deviation without prompting, adjusted power and re-established the profile before Low Key.
texts.3: SP monitored the deceleration and lowered the gear and takeoff flaps as soon as the aircraft was below 147 KIAS, then maintained 120 KIAS minimum toward Low Key. Altitude stayed within 150 feet of the intended profile and 4 to 6 percent torque was set at Low Key. No catching up was required in the descending part of the pattern.
texts.4: SP anticipated the 147 KIAS gate, so gear and takeoff flaps went down immediately at the deceleration and the aircraft settled on 120 KIAS with no further speed correction. The profile to Low Key was flown within about 50 feet of the intended altitude and 4 to 6 percent torque was set at Low Key. The configuration sequence did not interrupt the lookout or the spacing check.
texts.marginal: SP configured inside the limits, but the gear and takeoff flaps were always selected at the last moment of the deceleration below 147 KIAS, and the speed toward Low Key drifted down close to the 120 KIAS minimum before power was added. The profile stayed inside tolerance only because of a further power adjustment later. SP is expected to configure as soon as the gate is reached so that the aircraft is stabilized well before Low Key.
